claims.text: The starting Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Mo alloy is a cast, single-phase FCC solid solution with a coarse grain size of approximately 47 μm.
Severe plastic deformation followed by low-temperature annealing can produce grains below 50 nm and an FCC+HCP dual-phase structure in the Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Mo alloy.
High-pressure torsion or equal-channel angular pressing is an appropriate severe-plastic-deformation route for the proposed alloy.
Annealing at 600–700 °C for 1–2 hours will establish the desired nanocrystalline dual-phase microstructure.
An SPD strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 is suitable for producing the proposed microstructure.
SPD refines the grains to below 50 nm.
Controlled annealing promotes a partial FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries and FCC/HCP phase interfaces impede dislocation motion.
Grain-boundary and phase-boundary strengthening act synergistically to increase hardness and yield strength.
The processing route will increase yield strength by more than 300 MPa and hardness by more than 150 HV relative to the cast state.
The processed material will retain more than 20% tensile elongation.
No brittle intermetallic phase will form during the proposed processing route.
Suppressed diffusion and entropy stabilization prevent intermetallic formation during processing.
Mo content must be below approximately 4 at.% to remain within the solid-solution limit and avoid Mo-carbide formation.
Adding carbon stabilizes FCC and suppresses excessive HCP transformation.
Carbon must be limited to 0.5 at.% to avoid carbide precipitation.
Annealing above 700 °C causes destabilizing grain growth and excessive HCP transformation.
The cast baseline has a yield strength of approximately 400 MPa and elongation of approximately 60%.
Annealing of severely deformed material can become unstable through phase precipitation at moderate temperatures or long treatment times.
Local composition fluctuations, SPD heterogeneity, and trace impurities may alter phase fractions, grain-size distributions, or intermetallic formation.

contradictions.description: The stated starting alloy contains Mo5, whereas the hypothesis requires Mo to be kept below approximately 4 at.% to avoid carbide formation and remain within the asserted solid-solution limit. No compositional-adjustment step is included in the intervention.
Carbon addition is presented as necessary for FCC stabilization, but the intervention only specifies SPD and annealing and does not include a carbon-alloying step.
